title: Passing by value or by reference
objectives: Choose between a copy and a reference for each argument.
Predict whether a function call changes the caller's object.

screens.title: Who changes the vector
screens.question: What does the C++ program print?

options.why: You read it as Python, where the call shares the list. In C++ `costs` is a new vector, copied from `mine` when the call starts.
`costs` starts as a full copy of `mine`, and nothing ever empties `mine`.
It compiles. A parameter of type `std::vector<double>` simply receives a copy of the argument.

hints.text: Is `costs` the caller's vector, or a vector of its own?
Look at the parameter type. It has no `&` or anything else after the type.
`costs` is built as a copy of `mine`. `push_back` grows the copy, which is destroyed at the closing brace. `mine` keeps its two prices.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether `costs` is `mine` itself or a copy of it.

byKey.three: You read it as Python, where the call shares the list. In C++ `costs` is a new vector, copied from `mine`.

explain.text: `costs` is a separate vector, copied from `mine` when the call starts. `push_back` grows that copy, and the copy is destroyed at the function's closing brace. So `mine.size()` is still 2.

screens.title: Names on boxes

state.caption: The two vector objects after the last line

screens.question: Drag each name onto the box it names after the last line.

hints.text: Which line builds a second vector? The other names share the first one.
`copy` has no `&`, so it is a new box.
`mine` and `alias` name the box that `push_back` grew. `copy` names its own box, still `{250, 120}`.

feedback.correct: `mine` and `alias` name one box; `copy` is its own.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Only a declaration without `&` builds a new box.

byKey.mine: `mine` is the box the vector was built in, and the `push_back` through `alias` grew it.
byKey.alias: `alias` was declared with `&`, so it names the box `mine` already names. No new vector is made.
byKey.copy: `copy` has no `&`, so it is a new box, filled with `mine`'s two prices before the push.

explain.text: `alias` is a second name for `mine`'s box, so pushing through `alias` grew that box. `copy` is its own box, copied before the push, so it still holds two prices.

screens.title: A reference parameter

state.caption: During the call: `balance` and `cash` name one `double`

screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: That is what happens without the `&`. Here `balance` is another name for `cash`, so `balance -= fee` changes `cash`.
`balance -= fee` subtracts the fee from the balance. It does not replace the balance with the fee.
The value is right, but `std::cout` prints a `double` without trailing zeros unless you ask for fixed decimals.

hints.text: Is `balance` a copy of `cash`, or another name for it?
Both `cash` and `balance` point at the same box.
`balance -= fee` changes the one `double` that both names share: 1000 minus 2.5 is 997.5.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the arrows: which box does `balance -= fee` change?

byKey.unchanged: That is what happens without the `&`. Here `balance` is another name for `cash`, so `cash` changes.

explain.text: `balance` is a reference, so it names the same `double` as `cash`. Subtracting 2.50 through `balance` changes that one `double` to 997.5. `fee` has no `&`: it is a copy of 2.50, and changing it would not touch the caller.

screens.title: Read without copying
screens.prose: `prices` holds 1,000,000 prices, and `mean` only reads them. We want `v` to be a second name for `prices`, and we want the compiler to stop `mean` changing it. The keyword `const` means read only.

state.caption: Which parameter type joins `v` to this box, read only?

screens.question: Which signature should `mean` have?

options.why: That builds a second box and copies all 1,000,000 prices into it on every call.
That shares the box, but it lets `mean` change the prices, and the compiler will not stop it.
`const` stops changes, but without `&` this is still a full copy of the million prices.

hints.text: Two things are needed: no copy, and no changes.
`&` gives the sharing. What gives the read only part?
`const std::vector<double>&` is a reference, so nothing is copied, and `const` makes `v` read only.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the type that has both `&` and `const`.

byKey.value: That copies all 1,000,000 prices into `v` on every call.
byKey.cvalue: Without `&` this is still a copy, even if it is a read-only one.

explain.text: `const std::vector<double>& v` makes `v` a second name for `prices`, so nothing is copied. `const` means the compiler rejects any line in `mean` that would change it.

canvas.caption: `v` names the same box; the dashed arrow is read only

screens.title: What a copy costs
screens.prose: A `double` takes 8 bytes. Passing a vector by value copies every element into a new buffer. The table shows timings from this browser build.

state.caption: A `const&` call took a few nanoseconds at every size: nothing is copied.

screens.question: How many megabytes does one by-value call copy for 1,000,000 prices? Take 1 MB as 1,000,000 bytes.

widget.label: Megabytes copied
widget.accept: 8 MB: 1,000,000 prices times 8 bytes is 8,000,000 bytes.

hints.text: Each price is 8 bytes. How many bytes is a million of them?
Follow the column: each row multiplies the number of prices by 8.
1,000,000 times 8 bytes is 8,000,000 bytes, which is 8 MB.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the number of prices by 8 bytes, then convert to MB.

byKey.bytes: That is the count in bytes. Divide by 1,000,000 to get megabytes.
byKey.one: That counts one byte per price. A `double` takes 8.
byKey.bits: You multiplied by 64, the bits in a `double`. Count bytes: 8 each.

explain.text: Each of the 1,000,000 prices takes 8 bytes, so a by-value call copies 8,000,000 bytes, which is 8 MB. Here that takes about a millisecond per call. A pricing loop that calls it 1,000 times a second would spend its whole second copying.

screens.title: Your first const reference
screens.prose: A book holds share quantities and their prices in £, one entry per stock. Its value is the sum of quantity times price.
screens.question: Write `double total_value(...)` with both vectors passed by `const` reference.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and compiles in 10 to 15 s. Later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 5 hidden tests, including an empty book, a short position and a million-stock book. A hidden check after your code also tests the signature itself.

hints.text: Start with the signature: two `const std::vector<double>&` parameters, returning `double`.
Loop over the indices with `std::size_t i` from 0 to `qty.size()`.
Set `double total = 0;`, add `qty[i] * px[i]` for each `i`, then `return total;`. An empty book returns 0.

feedback.correct: Both vectors are read in place; nothing is copied.
feedback.generic: Not yet. The results under the editor say which test failed.

explain.text: `const std::vector<double>&` hands the function the caller's vectors without copying them. The loop only reads, so `const` costs nothing. An empty book never enters the loop and returns 0.

screens.title: The missing ampersand

state.caption: Two boxes: the parameter has no `&`

screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: You assumed the call changes the caller's vector. Without `&`, `normalise` divides its own copy, which is then destroyed.
It compiles cleanly. Taking a vector by value is legal; it just copies.
`w[0]` is the first weight, 2, and nothing changed it in the caller.

hints.text: Which box does `x /= sum` divide?
`normalise`'s `w` is a separate box.
The parameter has no `&`, so the division happens in the copy. The caller's `w[0]` is still 2.

feedback.correct: The copy was normalised; the caller's weights were not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check whether `normalise`'s `w` is the caller's vector or a copy.

byKey.fifth: You assumed the call changes the caller's vector. Without `&`, `normalise` divides its own copy, which is then destroyed.

explain.text: `normalise` divided its own copy, `{0.2, 0.3, 0.5}`, and that copy died at the closing brace. The caller's `w` is untouched, so `w[0]` prints 2. The compiler cannot warn you: copying is legal.

screens.title: Fix normalise
screens.prose: Fix `normalise` so it changes the caller's weights. Weights may be negative (a short position). If the weights sum to 0, or there are none, leave them as they are.
screens.question: Fix `normalise`.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and compiles in 10 to 15 s. Later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 6 hidden tests. Each builds a vector `w`, calls `normalise(w)`, then looks at `w` in the caller.

hints.text: Two fixes: the parameter type, and the case where the sum is 0.
Add `&` after the type so `w` names the caller's vector.
Write `std::vector<double>& w`. After summing, `if (sum == 0) return;` before dividing.

feedback.correct: The caller's weights now add up to 1.
feedback.generic: Not yet. The results under the editor say which test failed.

explain.text: With `std::vector<double>& w`, every `x /= sum` divides the caller's own weights. The early `return` avoids dividing by zero, which would turn every weight into `nan` or infinity. An empty vector sums to 0, so it returns at once.

screens.title: Three ways to pass
screens.prose:
Each parameter type says what the function will do with your object.

```cpp
void f(std::vector<double> v);         // its own copy
void f(const std::vector<double>& v);  // shared, read only
void f(std::vector<double>& v);        // shared, may change it
std::vector<double> g();               // returned, not copied
```

Returning a local by value is cheap. The compiler usually builds it in the caller's variable, and otherwise moves it. Either way no element is copied. Building it in place is **copy elision**.
screens.question: A function reads 1,000,000 prices and returns their mean. Which parameter fits?

options.why: That copies 8 MB on every call, only to read it.
That compiles, but it claims the function may change the prices, and it rejects temporaries and `const` vectors.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The function only reads, and the vector is large.

explain.text: A function that only reads a large object takes it by `const&`. Small values such as `double` and `int` go by value: copying 8 bytes is as cheap as sharing.

screens.title: Swap by reference
screens.prose:
Two reference parameters let one function change two of the caller's variables. Here `a` and `b` are the caller's bid and ask.

```cpp
void swap_px(double& a, double& b) {
    double t = a;   // keep the old a
    ________        // missing line
    b = t;          // b gets the old a
}
```
screens.question: Which line completes `swap_px`?

options.why: That copies `a` into `b`, so the old `b` is lost and both end up as the old `a`.
`t` holds the old `a`. Overwriting it loses that value, and `a` never changes.
`t` is a copy of `a`, so this writes `a` back into itself and changes nothing.

hints.text: After the first line, `t` keeps the old `a`. What should `a` become?
Each line has one job: save `a`, then overwrite `a`, then fill `b`.
`a` should take `b`'s value, which is safe because `t` saved the old `a`. Then `b = t` finishes the swap.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. After saving `a` in `t`, which variable can be overwritten safely?

byKey.ba: That copies `a` into `b` before `b` is saved, so the old `b` is lost.

explain.text: Line 1 saves the old `a` in `t`. Line 2 overwrites `a` with `b`, which is safe because `t` holds the old value. Line 3 gives `b` the old `a`; both writes reach the caller through the references.

screens.title: A risk engine's signature
screens.prose: A risk engine revalues a desk 1,000 times a second. The order book has 50,000 price levels and is only read. Every position's P&L is updated in place.
screens.question: Which signature should `revalue` have?

options.why: That copies the whole book 1,000 times a second. Every P&L update lands in a copy the caller never sees.
The `const` is on the wrong argument. The P&L updates will not compile, and the book could be changed by mistake.
The positions are right, but `const OrderBook` without `&` still copies 50,000 levels on every call.

hints.text: Ask two questions per argument: is it large, and does the function change it?
The book is large and read only. The positions are changed and must reach the caller.
Book: `const OrderBook&`. Positions: `std::vector<Position>&`.

feedback.correct: Read the book in place; change the positions in place.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. One argument is read only; the other must be changed for the caller.

byKey.copies: Both arguments are copied, so the P&L updates are lost.
byKey.swapped: The `const` belongs on the book, which is only read.

explain.text: The book is large and only read, so `const OrderBook&` shares it at no cost. The positions must change for the caller, so they go by plain `&`. Any line that wrote to the book would now be a compile error.

ideas: A C++ variable is its object. Passing by value gives the function its own copy; `T&` passes a second name for the caller's object.
`const T&` shares without copying and promises not to change; it also accepts temporaries such as `{1.0, 2.0}`. A plain `T&` may change the caller's object and needs a real variable.
Return results by value: the compiler builds them in the caller's variable, so a returned vector is not copied.

formula.name: Choosing a parameter
formula.note: Small types such as `int` and `double` go by value. Vectors and strings go by `const&` unless the function must change them.

summary.trap: Forgetting `&` compiles cleanly: the function changes its own copy and the caller sees nothing.

quiz.question: What does it print?

options.why: You read `r2` as a copy of `r`. A reference made from a reference names the same object, `x`.
`int& r2 = r;` is fine: `r` is just another name for `x`, so `r2` is a third one.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does `r` name?

explain.text: `r` names `x`, so `int& r2 = r;` makes `r2` name `x` too. There is no reference to a reference: `r2 = 9` writes to `x`.

quiz.question: What happens when you build this?

options.text: It does not compile: a plain `double&` cannot bind to the temporary `100.0`

options.why: A non-const reference must name a real variable. `100.0` is a temporary, so the call is rejected.

options.text: It compiles and changes a hidden copy
options.why: C++ will not make a hidden copy for a plain `&`. That is exactly why the call is an error.

feedback.correct: A plain reference needs a variable to change.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What would `balance -= fee` change here?

explain.text: `apply_fee` promises to change its first argument, so the argument must be a variable. clang says "expects an lvalue for 1st argument". A `const double&` parameter would accept `100.0`.

quiz.question: How many times are the 1,000,000 prices copied when `make_prices` returns?

options.text: None: the vector is built in `px` itself, or moved there

options.why: That was the worry before copy elision. The compiler builds `v` in `px`, or else moves it, so no price is copied.

options.text: Twice, into a temporary and then into `px`
options.why: The compiler removes both copies. A returned local vector is built in place or moved, never copied element by element.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does copy elision do with a returned local?

explain.text: The compiler usually builds `v` in the caller's `px` from the start; when it does not, it moves `v`. Either way no price is copied. That is why functions return vectors by value rather than through a reference parameter.

quiz.question: Which C++ parameter behaves like Python's `def add(costs): costs.append(1.5)`?

options.why: That is C++'s default, a copy. Python's call shares the caller's list.
It shares, but `const` forbids `push_back`, so the append would not compile.

feedback.correct: A plain reference shares and allows changes, as Python does.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Python shares the list and lets the function change it.

explain.text: A Python call shares the caller's list and may change it. In C++ that needs `&` without `const`. Without the `&`, C++ copies.
